articles.title: After Major Weight Loss, the Drug Wasn’t Enough — It Was Exercise That Healed the Arteries
articles.excerpt: In a year-long trial of adults who had already shed a tenth of their body weight, regular exercise measurably thinned artery walls and cooled inflammation — while the popular weight-loss drug liraglutide, taken on its own, did neither.
articles.image_caption: In a year-long trial, regular exercise — not the weight-loss drug liraglutide alone — improved artery health and lowered inflammation after major weight loss
articles.nri_angle: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are spreading fast through affluent diaspora circles as a shortcut around a stubborn metabolic burden — South Asians face heart disease earlier and at lower body weights than almost any group — yet this trial warns that the needle and the scale are not the whole story: the arterial and inflammatory protection NRIs most need came from movement, not the medication, a crucial caveat for a community quick to adopt the drugs but slow to keep up the exercise.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Joint-Pain Supplement Millions Take Daily Is Now Linked to Faster Dementia and Higher Death Risk
articles.excerpt: A large analysis of health records found that people with cognitive decline who took glucosamine were 25 percent more likely to progress to dementia — and those who already had it faced a 25 percent higher risk of dying — raising a clinical question researchers say now deserves far more attention.
articles.image_caption: Glucosamine, taken by tens of millions for joint pain, was linked to faster dementia progression and higher death risk in a large records analysis
articles.nri_angle: Glucosamine is a fixture in the daily supplement routines of aging Indians at home and abroad — taken on faith for creaky knees and passed between relatives like sound advice — even as South Asians carry a heavy, often early-onset dementia burden; this finding gives NRI families a concrete, time-sensitive reason to revisit what their parents are swallowing every morning, and to raise it with a doctor rather than the family WhatsApp group.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Genes May Decide Whether Your Sleep Protects Your Brain — or Harms It
articles.excerpt: A study of older Australians found that variants of a single gene governing the brain’s overnight waste-clearance system interact with sleep habits to shape brain structure and memory long before Alzheimer’s appears — meaning the same night’s sleep can help one person and hurt another.
articles.image_caption: Whether a given sleep pattern protects the aging brain may depend on a gene that governs its overnight waste-clearance system, researchers found
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry a heavy, often early-onset burden of dementia risk, and the diaspora’s sandwich generation — caring for aging parents while raising children — is hungry for concrete prevention advice; this study’s message that there is no universal ‘right’ amount of sleep, and that the benefit depends on your genes, argues for personalized, genetically informed brain care rather than one-size-fits-all rules NRI families often pass around.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Lifting Weights Through Midlife Sharply Cut the Risk of Type 2 Diabetes — Especially Paired With Walking
articles.excerpt: Following nearly 144,000 health professionals for almost two decades, researchers found that those who kept up resistance training had a markedly lower risk of type 2 diabetes — and the benefit was greatest when strength work was combined with aerobic exercise and less time in front of the television.
articles.image_caption: Consistent resistance training through midlife was linked to a sharply lower risk of type 2 diabetes, a 144,000-person study found
articles.nri_angle: South Asians develop type 2 diabetes earlier, at lower body weights, and at far higher rates than most other groups — a defining health threat for the Indian diaspora — yet the community’s exercise culture still leans heavily on walking and cardio while neglecting strength work; this study makes a data-backed case that adding resistance training, not just doing more cardio, is one of the most powerful levers NRIs and their families have against a disease that stalks them disproportionately.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Four Minutes a Day: A Tiny Strength Routine Sharply Improved Balance and Leg Power in Older Adults
articles.excerpt: A home workout of just four exercises, 30 seconds each, left frail adults over 65 stronger and steadier on their feet after 12 weeks — a low-barrier answer to the falls that are among the leading causes of death in old age, Penn State researchers report.
articles.image_caption: A short, home-based strength routine improved balance and leg power in adults over 65, a Penn State trial found
articles.nri_angle: Aging Indian parents and grandparents — often living with NRI children abroad or alone back home while their families are overseas — are exactly the group most at risk from falls and least likely to take up a gym routine, so a free, four-minute, equipment-light workout that can be coached over video and done in a living room offers diaspora families a realistic way to protect elders' independence across distance.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Weight Comes Back. Exercise May Be the Quiet Reason It Comes Back Less
articles.excerpt: Pooling 11 clinical trials, researchers found that people who exercised during the maintenance phase after losing weight — through dieting, drugs or surgery — regained nearly three kilograms less than those who did not, a timely finding in the age of weight-loss injections.
articles.image_caption: Exercise during the weight-maintenance phase was linked to less weight regain after dieting or surgery
articles.nri_angle: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are spreading fast among affluent, health-conscious NRIs and urban Indians alike, and the hardest question — what happens when you stop, and the weight creeps back on a body already prone to diabetes and heart disease — is one this study speaks to directly, suggesting the cheapest, most durable insurance against regain is a habit of regular movement, not another prescription.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Five Minutes Every Hour: A Simple Movement Habit Lifted Mood and Cut Fatigue, a Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Short walking breaks scattered through the workday eased fatigue and brightened mood in nearly 11,500 adults — and, contrary to the fear that stepping away hurts output, work performance edged up rather than down, researchers report.
articles.image_caption: People out for a brisk walk. A new study finds five-minute movement breaks each hour lift mood and cut fatigue (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: A large share of the Indian diaspora works in desk-bound technology, finance and professional jobs where ten-hour sitting days are routine, layered on a genetic predisposition to early heart disease and diabetes — so a study showing that five-minute walking breaks an hour, with no gym and no lost productivity, can lift mood and break up dangerous sitting offers NRI knowledge workers a free, frictionless lever for both mind and metabolism.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It May Not Be How Many Fruits You Eat, but Which Ones — a 30,000-Person Study Points to the Heart
articles.excerpt: Fewer than one in five people get enough flavanols, the heart-friendly compounds concentrated in apples with their skin, berries, plums, broad beans and green tea — even among those who dutifully hit their five-a-day, an international study using blood and urine markers finds.
articles.image_caption: Berries, apples with their skins and green tea are among the foods richest in heart-friendly flavanols
articles.nri_angle: Indian diaspora kitchens lean heavily on mangoes, bananas and citrus while the quietly flavanol-rich foods — apples eaten with the skin, berries, plums, broad beans and green tea — often sit at the edges of the plate, so a study showing it is the specific foods, not just the serving count, that protect the heart gives health-conscious NRI families a precise, low-cost lever against a community already prone to early cardiovascular disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Weight-Loss Pill, Taken Any Time of Day, Shed Up to 12% in a Year in an Early Trial
articles.excerpt: An experimental oral GLP-1 drug, aleniglipron, helped overweight and obese adults lose as much as 12 percent of their body weight over 36 weeks with few side effects — and, unusually, can be swallowed at any time without the strict fasting rules of existing pills.
articles.image_caption: An experimental oral GLP-1 pill helped adults lose up to 12 percent of body weight in an early trial
articles.nri_angle: Obesity and type 2 diabetes strike the Indian diaspora earlier and at lower body weights than many other groups, yet injectable weight-loss drugs are costly and off-putting — so a cheap-to-make oral GLP-1 that works without injections or rigid fasting rules could matter enormously for NRI families, especially as India's generic industry stands ready to mass-produce such pills.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The 'Sunshine Vitamin' Many Are Missing — Even in Summer, and Most of All Those With Darker Skin
articles.excerpt: New research finds large numbers of people run low on vitamin D year-round without knowing it — nearly three in four with darker skin pigmentation in one study — just as a separate trial suggests that getting levels right can sharply cut heart-attack risk.
articles.image_caption: New research finds vitamin D deficiency is common year-round, especially among people with darker skin pigmentation
articles.nri_angle: Vitamin D is made in the skin from sunlight, and darker skin makes far less of it — so Indian-origin families living in the cloudier, higher-latitude cities of the US, UK and Canada are among the most likely in the world to be quietly deficient, a risk that compounds the community's existing vulnerability to diabetes and heart disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: For Those With Alzheimer's in the Family, One Eating Pattern Stood Out, a New Analysis Finds
articles.excerpt: Among people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's, researchers found that an anti-inflammatory diet — not a Mediterranean or a generally 'healthy' one — was the only pattern tied to a meaningfully lower risk, pointing to inflammation as a lever the high-risk can pull.
articles.image_caption: An anti-inflammatory diet rich in leafy greens, berries and legumes was tied to lower Alzheimer's risk in the genetically predisposed
articles.nri_angle: Alzheimer's and dementia run in many Indian families, and the community already carries a high genetic and metabolic risk — so a finding that the predisposed may benefit most from a specifically anti-inflammatory diet, one that maps neatly onto traditional Indian staples like lentils, leafy greens, turmeric and vegetables, offers an actionable lever rather than a fatalistic shrug.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Single Habit — Regular Exercise — May Head Off Nearly Half of Dementia Cases, Researchers Say
articles.excerpt: Of the fourteen lifestyle and environmental factors that shape dementia risk, six can be tackled through exercise alone, University of Minnesota researchers report — and a virtual program shows even rural adults far from gyms can do it from home.
articles.image_caption: Researchers say regular exercise can address six of the fourteen modifiable risk factors for dementia
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry an elevated, earlier risk of both diabetes and dementia, and aging diaspora parents are often scattered far from family and specialist care — so a finding that one accessible, no-cost habit, deliverable even by telehealth at home, can address six of dementia's biggest risk factors is unusually relevant to Indian-origin households.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Three Everyday Sleep Habits May Be Quietly Aging the Brain, a 23,000-Person Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Sleeping outside the recommended seven-to-nine-hour window, napping often during the day and struggling with sleeplessness were each linked to more of the brain damage that builds up with age — and all three, researchers note, can be changed.
articles.image_caption: A study of 23,000 middle-aged and older adults links three common sleep habits to brain aging
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin professionals abroad routinely run on short, broken sleep — late video calls with family in India, demanding jobs across time zones, the cultural habit of the afternoon nap — so evidence that these specific patterns may accelerate brain aging hands the diaspora a concrete, no-cost lever to protect long-term cognitive health.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Even 'Safe' Air May Be Hardening the Heart's Arteries, a Large Imaging Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Scanning the hearts of more than 11,000 adults, researchers found that long-term exposure to air pollution — even at levels below regulatory limits — was tied to more advanced coronary artery disease, with women facing a markedly higher risk.
articles.image_caption: A large imaging study tied long-term air pollution, even at safe levels, to more advanced coronary artery disease
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin families straddle two air-quality worlds — long stays in some of the planet's most polluted cities back home and daily life in Western suburbs assumed to be clean — so a finding that even 'safe' air damages arteries reframes pollution as a heart risk the diaspora carries in both places, on top of an already high genetic burden of cardiovascular disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It May Not Be How Much You Move, but How Many Ways — Exercise Variety Is Linked to a Longer Life
articles.excerpt: A large analysis finds that people who mix walking, lifting, cycling and other activities have lower death rates than those who rely on a single form of exercise — even after accounting for how much they do in total.
articles.image_caption: A new analysis links variety in physical activity, not just total volume, to lower mortality
articles.nri_angle: Many in the Indian diaspora settle into one fitness rut — the daily treadmill walk, the weekend cricket match, the gym routine that never changes — so evidence that mixing activity types adds years, independent of how much you do, offers a practical, low-cost upgrade for busy NRI households trying to outrun the community’s high cardiometabolic risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Plant-Forward Mediterranean Diet Was Tied to a 26% Lower Heart-Disease Risk Over 20 Years, a Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Following more than 3,000 Greek adults for two decades, researchers found that those who ate the most vegetables, fruit, legumes, grains and fish had dramatically lower cardiovascular risk — while calorie-heavy diets light on lean meat fared worst.
articles.image_caption: A plant-forward Mediterranean diet of vegetables, legumes, grains and fish was tied to lower 20-year heart-disease risk
articles.nri_angle: A plant-forward pattern built on vegetables, legumes, whole grains and fish maps closely onto traditional Indian vegetarian and coastal cooking — so for a diaspora whose diets have drifted toward calorie-dense, processed convenience food abroad, this 20-year evidence is a reminder that the heart-protective template may already sit in their own kitchens.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It Isn't Being Alone That Ages the Mind — It's Feeling Lonely, a 175,000-Person Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Drawing on data from 18 countries, researchers found that the perception of loneliness, far more than simply living a solitary life, predicted faster cognitive decline and a shorter life — a distinction with real consequences for how families care for ageing parents.
articles.image_caption: A 175,000-person study across 18 countries found feeling lonely, more than living alone, tracks with faster cognitive decline (Openverse)
articles.nri_angle: For Indian families spread across continents — children in the US or UK, parents back home — this study reframes the worry: a grandparent who lives alone but feels connected may fare far better than one surrounded by people yet quietly lonely, a nuance that should reshape how the diaspora thinks about long-distance caregiving.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cholesterol Pills May Touch More Than the Heart — a Genetic Study Maps Effects on Weight, Hormones and the Brain
articles.excerpt: Using DNA rather than years of follow-up, Australian researchers found that statins and the newer PCSK9 inhibitors carry distinct side-effect signatures — from body fat and testosterone to lung function and even brain size — a reminder that two drugs aimed at the same target are not interchangeable.
articles.image_caption: A genetic study finds statins and PCSK9 inhibitors carry distinct effects beyond cholesterol, from weight and hormones to lung and brain
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry one of the world's highest burdens of early heart disease, and statins are a fixture in many NRI households; this study is a nudge to treat cholesterol medication as a personalised decision — worth a real conversation with a doctor — rather than a one-size-fits-all pill.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Poor Sleep in the Teenage Years Casts a Long Shadow Into Adulthood, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Tracking young people from age 15 to 22, researchers found that irregular sleep and insomnia symptoms as a teenager predicted worse health, more hospital stays and lower life satisfaction years later — evidence that adolescent sleep is an investment, not a luxury.
articles.image_caption: Researchers tracked young people from age 15 to 22, linking poor teenage sleep to worse adult health
articles.nri_angle: In high-achieving Indian and South Asian households, late-night study, packed extracurriculars and the quiet glorification of running on little sleep are common among teenagers chasing top grades and college admissions — so evidence that adolescent sleep shapes health and wellbeing for years afterward speaks directly to how diaspora families weigh academic pressure against rest.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cutting Out Sugar Entirely May Backfire, a New Study Warns — Balance Beats Elimination
articles.excerpt: In a 16-week experiment, animals fed a low-fat diet stripped of all table sugar developed gut imbalance, insulin resistance and early fatty-liver changes — even though they gained no extra weight. The lesson, researchers say, is that the body needs balanced carbohydrates, not a zero.
articles.image_caption: A 16-week study found that a low-fat diet with all table sugar removed harmed gut and metabolic health in mice
articles.nri_angle: Sugar has become the villain of choice in diaspora wellness circles — 'no-sugar' challenges, sugar-free mithai and zero-sugar swaps are everywhere among health-conscious NRIs guarding against the community’s steep diabetes risk — so a study suggesting that total elimination can harm gut and metabolic health is a timely reminder that balance, not a blanket ban, is what protects the body.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: For Yo-Yo Dieters, the Trick May Be When You Eat, Not How Much You Count
articles.excerpt: An 18-month Australian trial found intermittent fasting matched old-fashioned calorie counting for weight loss — but felt far easier, because dieters never had to police every mouthful. About a sixth of their success came down to that lighter mental load alone.
articles.image_caption: An 18-month Australian trial found intermittent fasting matched calorie counting for weight loss but felt easier to sustain
articles.nri_angle: In Indian and South Asian homes food is love, hospitality and ritual — the calorie-counting diet, with its weighing of every roti and ladoo, collides head-on with that culture, which is exactly why a fasting approach the community already knows from vrat and Ekadashi may prove far easier to live with.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Strict Low-Carb Diet Eased Hard-to-Treat Depression in a New Trial — but Doctors Urge Caution
articles.excerpt: In a UK study of people whose depression had resisted standard treatment, six weeks on a ketogenic diet brought a slightly bigger drop in symptoms than a healthy comparison diet — a tantalising hint that what we eat may reach the brain, not just the body.
articles.image_caption: A UK trial tested a strict ketogenic diet against a healthy comparison diet in people with treatment-resistant depression
articles.nri_angle: Depression remains heavily stigmatised in many Indian and South Asian families, where it is often hidden or dismissed rather than treated — so any evidence that a dietary change, framed as wellness rather than illness, can ease symptoms may reach people who would never walk into a psychiatrist’s office.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Three Years of Diet and Exercise Paid Off for Two Decades — Far Beyond Diabetes, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: People with prediabetes who followed an intensive diet-and-exercise program were 21% less likely to pile up multiple chronic diseases over the next 20-plus years — and the protection held even after diabetes itself was taken out of the equation.
articles.image_caption: A new study finds a few years of diet and exercise can cut chronic-disease risk for decades (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: South Asians slide from prediabetes to diabetes faster and younger than most populations, and rarely stop there — heart disease, kidney trouble and more tend to stack up; this study shows a few years of disciplined diet and movement at the prediabetes stage can blunt that whole cascade decades later, not just the diabetes.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Lifting Weights Just an Hour or Two a Week Is Linked to a Longer Life, a 30-Year Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Tracking nearly 150,000 people for three decades, researchers found a clear sweet spot — about 90 to 120 minutes of strength training a week — tied to lower death rates, with the biggest gains against heart disease and dementia when weights were paired with everyday aerobic activity.
articles.image_caption: A 30-year study of nearly 150,000 people links one to two hours of weekly strength training to a longer life
articles.nri_angle: Strength training is still rare in many Indian and South Asian households — walking is the default, the gym is seen as vanity, and women in particular are often steered away from weights — yet this is precisely the community that carries an outsized burden of diabetes and heart disease that building muscle helps blunt.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Aging Doesn't Have to Mean Decline — Nearly Half of Older Adults Got Sharper or Stronger, a Yale Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Tracking more than 11,000 older Americans for over a decade, Yale researchers found that 45 percent improved in memory, mobility, or both — and the people most likely to gain were those who held a more hopeful view of growing old.
articles.image_caption: A new Yale study finds nearly half of adults over 65 improved in memory, mobility, or both — with a hopeful view of aging a key factor
articles.nri_angle: Many Indian diaspora families care for ageing parents and grandparents across continents, and the cultural script of later life is often one of inevitable frailty and dependence; this study suggests that mindset itself shapes how elders age — a reason to treat older relatives as capable of growth rather than quietly writing off their decline.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: One Question — 'How Old Do You Feel?' — May Reveal Whether You're Sleeping Well Enough
articles.excerpt: A new study of more than 3,100 adults finds that people who feel older than their actual age tend to sleep worse, pointing to a single, disarmingly simple cue that something may be off with your rest.
articles.image_caption: A new study links feeling older than one's age to poorer sleep, offering a simple self-check on whether the body is getting enough rest
articles.nri_angle: Sleep is the quiet casualty of immigrant life — long commutes, late shifts, calls timed to family in India, and the grind of building a life in a new country all erode it; this research hands the diaspora a free, instant self-check on whether that chronic rest deficit is catching up with them.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Lifting Weights, Not Just Walking, May Be the Missing Piece in Holding Off Diabetes
articles.excerpt: Tracking nearly 144,000 adults for almost two decades, researchers found that regular strength training cut the risk of type 2 diabetes — and pairing it with aerobic exercise and less screen time cut that risk by more than half.
articles.image_caption: A new 144,000-person study links regular strength training, alongside aerobic exercise, to a sharply lower risk of type 2 diabetes
articles.nri_angle: South Asians develop type 2 diabetes earlier, at lower body weights, and at far higher rates than most populations — yet exercise in many diaspora households still means a walk, if anything, with strength training seen as optional or vain; this study reframes resistance work as a core piece of prevention for the community most at risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It May Not Be How Much Fat You Eat, but Which Kind — a Diabetes Review Shifts the Blame
articles.excerpt: Scientists reviewing the molecular evidence argue that palmitic acid, common in palm oil, fried food and baked goods, quietly sabotages insulin, while the oleic acid in olive oil and nuts may shield against it — pointing to fat quality, not quantity, as the real lever.
articles.image_caption: A new review argues the type of fat — olive oil's oleic acid versus palm oil's palmitic acid — matters more than the amount for diabetes risk
articles.nri_angle: Palm oil and reused frying oil are everywhere in the Indian diaspora's kitchens and takeaways — in packaged snacks, sweets, namkeen and restaurant fryers — making palmitic acid an unusually heavy presence in desi diets already burdened by sky-high diabetes rates; this review suggests swapping the oil, not just cutting the fat, could matter more than calorie-counting.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Hardest Part of Losing Weight Is Keeping It Off — a New Review Says Exercise Is the Glue
articles.excerpt: Pooling 11 clinical trials, researchers found that people who kept exercising after losing weight regained nearly three kilograms less than those who stopped — a small but remarkably consistent edge in the war against the rebound.
articles.image_caption: A new meta-analysis finds staying active after weight loss helps prevent the kilos from creeping back
articles.nri_angle: Crash diets and quick weight loss before a wedding or a trip home are a familiar ritual in many Indian families — and so is the quiet return of the kilos months later; this review reframes the goal from losing weight to defending it, a message that matters for a diaspora facing high rates of diabetes and heart disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Mother's Heart Health Before Birth May Shape Her Child's Development, a Study of 8,000 Finds
articles.excerpt: Children of mothers with poor cardiovascular health had a 62% higher risk of developmental delay by age four — across communication, movement, problem-solving and social skills — pointing to pregnancy as one of the earliest windows to protect a child's future.
articles.image_caption: A study of 8,000 mothers links poor cardiovascular health in pregnancy to higher developmental-delay risk in children
articles.nri_angle: South Asian women carry unusually high rates of gestational diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, often undiagnosed, while pre-pregnancy health is rarely discussed in diaspora families fixated on the baby rather than the mother; this research makes a mother's own heart health a quiet but powerful lever over her child's lifelong development.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Simple Walk With Poles Eased Depression in Five Weeks, a New Trial Finds
articles.excerpt: In a randomized study of 64 adults with moderate-to-severe depression, a supervised Nordic-walking program brought large, rapid drops in symptoms within the first five weeks — and the most severely depressed improved the fastest.
articles.image_caption: A new randomized trial found supervised Nordic walking eased moderate-to-severe depression within five weeks
articles.nri_angle: Depression is heavily stigmatised and under-treated across many Indian families, where therapy and antidepressants are still met with shame or silence; a low-cost, group-friendly walk that shows benefit in weeks is the kind of accessible, face-saving first step that can reach diaspora elders and stressed newcomers who would never walk into a psychiatrist's office.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It Isn't Just the Calories: Ultra-Processed Diets Are Now Linked to Falling Male Fertility
articles.excerpt: A tightly controlled feeding study found that just three weeks on an ultra-processed diet worsened body fat, blood lipids and hormones tied to sperm production — even when calories and nutrients were matched — pointing the finger at industrial processing itself.
articles.image_caption: A controlled study links ultra-processed diets to hormonal changes affecting sperm production in young men
articles.nri_angle: Falling fertility and rising reliance on packaged convenience food are both acute in diaspora life — long work hours, ready meals and Western supermarket aisles displacing home-cooked dals and vegetables — making this a quietly personal warning for younger NRI couples already navigating the cost and stress of fertility treatment abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A High-Dose Omega-3 Pill Reached the Brain but Did Nothing for Memory, a Gold-Standard Trial Finds
articles.excerpt: In a two-year randomized trial of older adults at risk of dementia, daily fish-oil-style DHA more than doubled omega-3 levels in the blood and reached the brain — yet it failed to improve memory, thinking or the size of the brain’s memory centre any more than a placebo.
articles.image_caption: Omega-3 fish-oil capsules; a two-year randomized trial found high-dose DHA reached the brain but did not improve memory
articles.nri_angle: Fish-oil and omega-3 capsules are among the most popular over-the-counter supplements in Indian-origin households, often bought in bulk and taken for years in the belief they protect the aging brain; this rigorous trial is a reminder that for most people the money may be better spent on diet and exercise than on a daily pill.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It May Not Be How Much Protein You Eat, but Which Building Blocks — a New Longevity-Diet Study Suggests
articles.excerpt: Scientists at USC report that fine-tuning a single amino acid, methionine, let mice eat more food yet lose fat without losing muscle — and that people eating the most animal protein had twice the rate of diabetes, hinting the kind of protein may matter more than the amount.
articles.image_caption: Lentils and legumes; new research suggests the type of protein, not just the amount, may shape metabolic health
articles.nri_angle: The protein debate cuts to the heart of diaspora eating habits — from the dal-and-rice plant-based traditions of many Indian households to the high-protein, meat-heavy regimes popular in Western fitness culture — and this research suggests the traditional emphasis on plant proteins may carry an underappreciated metabolic advantage.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
